name: Iṣẹkírì
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_citation: Osewa, Oludewa Roselyn & Osaigbovo Obed Evbuomwan. 2022. An Optimality Theoretic Analysis of the Mid Tone in Iṣẹkírì. Macrolinguistics 10(1) (Serial No. 16): 132-150. doi:10.26478/ja2022.10.16.6 (open access; cites Omamor 1979 'A phonological sketch of Isekir…
catalog_quote: Iṣẹkírì is a Yoruboid language, a member of the Benue-Congo family (Williamson, 1989), spoken in Warri and Sapele areas of Delta State, Nigeria (Lloyd, 1957:172; Sagey, 1981:10; Eyeoyibo, 2008:1; Ogharaerumi, 2010:1). The language is an example of a tone language (Yip, 2002:1; Yul-Ifode, 2008). ... Omamor (1979), Otokunefor (2002), Samuel (2011), Ijama (2014), Inoniyegha (2014), and Osewa (2016) examine the aspects of Iṣẹkírì phonology and establish its sound inventory and processes. On the prosodic level, Omamor (1979) and Osewa (2016) identify three level tones, H, M and L. They also identify the LL, MM and MH patterns for disyllabic nouns and H, M and L for monosyllabic verbs. Omamor (1979) notes that the L is the most unstable tone and usually deleted when in contact with the H or M.

new_statements.quote: The Iṣẹkírì language is classified as a Yoruboid language, a member of the Benue-Congo family within the Niger-Congo phylum (Williamson, 1988). Like the Yoruboid family of languages, it is tonal, and contrasts three level tones, like most dialects of modern Yoruba (Laniran, 1992; Akinlabi, 2000; Fajobi, 2005). Contour tones (rising and falling) are realized as a combination of two level tones; the high and low tones.
new_statements.citation: Osewa, O. R. & C. U. C. Ugorji. 2019. Tone in Iṣẹkírì: An Acoustic Investigation. Coaxial Journal of Linguistics Studies 2(1): 74-102.
new_statements.locator: p. 75 (p. 2), section 1 Introduction; same claim in the Abstract p. 74; conclusion p. 96-97
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (genuine 28-page PDF, Word-2016 text, Coaxial J. Ling. Studies 2(1) pp. 74-102; extracted text beside it; logs the RG not reachable by automated download and the the Internet Archive id_ download). The quoted passage is on p. 2 = printed p. 75, section 1 Introduction, verbatim (byte match after Unicode NFC normalisation of the combining under-dots; wording, punctuation and citations identical). The abstract (p. 74) repeats 'Like modern Yoruba, it is tonal and contrasts three level tones'; the conclusion (pp. 96-97, PDF 23-24) states the three-way H/M/L contrast, nouns essentially disyllabic VCV with only M or L on the initial syllable ('the High tone does not occur word initially'),…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Iṣẹkírì carries an empty rule and there are no existing stress statements. This work establishes the prosodic type: a tone language with three contrastive level tones (H, M, L), contour tones as H+L combinations, H barred from word-initial position in (VCV) nouns. It makes no statement about word stress or accent in Iṣẹkírì; the only occurrence of the word 'stress' (p. 77) is a generic definition of pitch/F0 ('tonal phenomena such as tone, stress and intonation'), not a claim about the language. Compatible with the catalog (nothing to contradict) and adds the tonal typing.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Iṣẹkírì is a tone language with three contrastive level tones (High, Mid, Low), acoustically validated from 338 words / six speakers; contours are H+L sequences; disyllabic (VCV) nouns allow only M or L on the first syllable (H never word-initial), giving LL, MM, MH noun patterns (p. 75-76, 96-97). No word-stress or accent system is described or mentioned for the language.
new_statements.exceptions: Tonal distribution restriction only: High tone does not occur word-initially on nouns (first syllable of VCV nouns is M or L; L-initial nouns are obligatorily LL) (p. 76, 96). Authors state there are no regional varieties of Iṣẹkírì (p. 75).
new_statements.identity_note: The work describes Iṣẹkírì (Itsekiri) as spoken in the Niger Delta, data from six native speakers recorded at the University of Benin and in the field; the authors state the language has no regional varieties ('monolithic', p. 75), so no dialect qualification applies.
